The same discretion helps explain the general absence of missionary zeal and attempts to win converts in Iranian Shiism. In that very circle, I recently heard a young mullah, about thirty years old, say with deep conviction that Shiism addresses everyone, but that only a spiritual minority can truly accept it, and that its task is to bring such people to light. The Imams themselves, he said, had understood this perfectly. How often I also heard it said: “If the Imam himself has not led you to these things, if the ability to understand them is not already within you, everything people tell you from the outside will fall on deaf ears.” We shall see that the idea of the Imam as an inward guide runs through the whole of Shiite spirituality.

Such an approach, founded on the spirit of initiation, is hardly designed to make scholarly research easy. Shiite literature is immense, in both Arabic and Persian, and includes printed books as well as vast stores of manuscripts. Demanding a complete reading list at the outset is not necessarily the best way to find your way through it. Books reveal themselves gradually: not only through long visits to libraries, whose catalogues are improving considerably, but also through friendly conversations and unexpected encounters. The same may happen with a celebrated pilgrimage site that you somehow never knew existed. Ask why no one told you about a particular book or place earlier, and the answer is almost always the same: only now was the time for you to discover it. Nothing happens by chance.

In short, perhaps even more than with other religious worlds, entering the spirit of Shiism and living within it requires becoming its spiritual guest. To be a guest in a spiritual world, however, you must first make room for it inside yourself. You can live in the Shiite spiritual world, and understand what it is like to live there, only if that world also lives within you. Without this inner participation, you can speak only from the outside, probably misunderstanding what you describe. No one can give a proper account of a building they have never entered.

The philosophers of illumination who follow Suhrawardi, known as the Ishraqiyun, insist that philosophy and spiritual life cannot be separated. In this they give Iranian Islamic thought one of its distinctive features.

But they also challenge the researcher to undertake a long spiritual journey. The guest they welcome cannot be a weekend visitor. They must become a long-term resident, and eventually something like an adopted member of the family, accepting the duties that come with belonging to the household. They may even be the first to recognise and describe a danger that threatens it. If so, they have a responsibility to help their new brothers and sisters face that danger, so that the house can continue to shelter everyone who comes to it for refuge.

It is, of course, an “esoteric” house. I know that the word esoteric is often misused in the West, and that Western readers have good reason to find it irritating when it is used to dress up thoroughly ordinary interests or social vanity. Here, though, I use it in a precise sense, to translate Arabic terms such as batin and ghayb. They describe a spiritual world inaccessible to ordinary sense perception or abstract reasoning. It is the inner, invisible world of the soul, the only world in which souls can truly offer one another hospitality. Spiritual traditions called esoteric bear witness, in their different ways, to the same hidden, inward realities that transcend our everyday world.

These traditions are forms of divine wisdom—what the Greek roots of theosophia literally mean. They converge on the goal of the same quest. The home of Wisdom, Domus Sapientiae, stands at the summit of the soul, wherever that summit is reached, just as the centre is present wherever one truly reaches the centre.

As the researcher goes deeper, the difficulties encountered on the Shiite side may be resolved through the energy of the search itself, when that search genuinely comes from the heart. I am less certain that the problems awaiting the researcher on the Western side will be so easily settled. Simplified explanations accepted long ago and repeated without question can prevent us from asking the new questions needed to enter this spiritual world. Sometimes it seems there is a strange determination to play down the meaning and importance of Shiite religious experience, as though recognising its spiritual foundations might threaten established academic or religious positions.

The researcher will also have to confront the effects of Western influence on a traditional civilisation—effects suffered first of all by their Shiite friends. There is a mysterious law: “Only the weapon that caused the wound can heal it.” Perhaps, if the West has produced the poison, it can also produce the antidote. But I am not sure it has yet recognised that responsibility. These difficulties deserve a closer look.

Religious experience—the perception of a religious reality—is a primary phenomenon (what German thinkers call an Urphänomen), like hearing a sound or seeing a colour. A primary experience is not something we explain by reducing it to something else. It is our starting point, something that helps us explain many other things. The weakness of philosophies that call themselves “positive,” and of approaches that hover around philosophy without really practising it, is that they try to derive religion from something else. They explain it through politics, society, ethnicity, economics, geography, or other circumstances, and in doing so miss what is uniquely religious about it.

We can pile up as many circumstances as we like, but they will never produce a particular religious experience unless there is first a consciousness that perceives it, that allows the religious reality to appear to itself. If a religion exists, its most basic reason for existing is that there are people who live and profess it. We achieve nothing by telling them, “You can disappear now. We've explained you.” Religious reality has a way of appearing again, freely and without warning: the Spirit blows where it wills. Its perception does not need to be justified by something outside itself.

The study of how things appear to consciousness, and of what we can know through that experience, is called phenomenology. It asks what something means when consciousness encounters it and gives it its place in the world. Yet considerable effort has been spent trying to explain—or rather reconstruct—Shiite religious experience by appealing to the assumptions of our modern Western view of life. Those assumptions may be completely foreign to religion as it is experienced.

I will return to this point. We have too often forgotten the primary fact of religious experience. We have forgotten that human beings shape their world and surroundings in response to their sense, however dim, of where they come from and where their lives are going. Instead, we take the reverse process for granted, assuming that their surroundings produce their deepest spiritual concerns. But it is the original religious experience that can explain those surroundings. How could someone see this, though, if they have lost the very ability to see it?

What we need to see is precisely what these explanations fail to reach. They gather all sorts of information already known from elsewhere and use it to “reconstruct” a religious reality that was there from the beginning. But no analysis could ever give us that reality if a consciousness had not first experienced it. We must try to see what the philosophers and spiritual teachers saw when they raised their questions and debated them.

How can we do that if we are not, in our own way, philosophers and spiritual seekers? What if we have forgotten what philosophical vision means, or surrendered philosophy's enduring right to ask its own questions, whatever the period in which we live? We make precisely that surrender when we mistake philosophy for the sociology of philosophy. Behind it lies a choice, stated openly or simply assumed, not to believe that the object of metaphysical inquiry exists at all. Metaphysics is treated as an illusion belonging to an outdated age. What interests us “scientifically,” so the argument goes, is people's social behaviour and the political circumstances that might explain why humanity spent so long pursuing the supposed illusion of religious and metaphysical truth.

But is it really scientific to explain to people who see something why they see it, when you yourself cannot see what they see? What can you know about the object of their vision if you cannot perceive it? For you, the object is simply nonexistent. How, then, can social circumstances explain that supposed nothing? When such explanations are applied to the intricate details of metaphysical systems—details often unknown to the people who dismiss them in advance—the results can be almost comical. Unfortunately, that does not stop the damage they cause.

In the West, we have tended to turn religious realities into social realities, driven by something like an urge to make them “incarnate” in visible, worldly forms. We prefer to study the historical answers people have given to a problem rather than reach the problem itself. We would rather explain religion as something other than itself than allow it to speak in its own terms. For all these reasons, and more, we have forgotten something basic about Islam: before anything else, it is a religion. Its source is a prophetic inspiration, and its Prophet experienced anew the scriptural revelations that came before his own.

Instead, some have tried to explain Islam in racial terms, identifying it with the Arab people and forgetting both the reach of Islam beyond the Arabic-speaking world and the devotion of non-Arab Muslims. Political ambition alone cannot turn an ethnic identity into the universal calling of a religion. Here and elsewhere, I have tried to clear up this confusion by explaining why we should speak of Islamic philosophy rather than Arab philosophy. This does not diminish the true greatness of the Arab contribution. On the contrary, it allows us to see it in relation to the Arab Prophet, as a prophetic greatness rising far above the limited ambitions of rulers and conquerors. It belongs to the divine realm, not to anything human beings can claim as their possession.

We can then recognise, without hesitation, the many Iranian thinkers who have shaped the history of Islamic philosophy and spirituality—not only in its first centuries, but from the seventeenth century right up to our own day. Its great works are written not just in classical Arabic but also in Persian. What emerges from this Iranian contribution is a spiritual world with a character of its own: Iranian Islam, with its Shiism, its philosophy of illumination (Ishraq), and its Sufi traditions.

But if we are serious about respecting religious experience, we must once again refuse an explanation based on ethnicity, as though mysterious “racial genes” somehow produced this spiritual world. Such an explanation would be no more convincing than an attempt to derive the form of Sunni Islam from an Arab “race.” In the end, what would any of this tell us about humanity's spiritual life?

This sort of explanation would leave us within the same fundamental refusal to recognise spiritual realities that I have already criticised. It would remain utterly foreign to the experience it claimed to explain. A simple example may help. In French, it seems perfectly natural to identify one part of Islam by adding a national label. The title of this book speaks of “Iranian Islam,” and I will also use the phrase “Iranian Shiism.” These categories seem obvious to us.

But translated literally into Persian, they would sound awkward, even offensive. Adding a national label in this way can seem to turn something sacred into something merely worldly. Iranian friends have pointed this out to me many times: a literal translation would sound strange and jarring. Perhaps what seems self-evident to us, with our focus on observable and practical categories, is alien to the spirit of these traditions. Are we not at risk of distorting something essential?

Rather than build explanations out of external causes, then, let us attend to spiritual experiences as they present themselves. Let us discover what religious life shows us, and what it can explain. In this case, the first thing we see is the extraordinary, wholehearted devotion of the Iranian soul to the Shiite idea, which it has made its own in a special way.

But when you give yourself entirely to something, it is truer to say that it has taken hold of you than that you possess it. Spiritual reality contains and surrounds us more than we contain it. Once we reverse our ordinary way of looking at the relationship between inner life and the world, the bond between Iran and Shiism takes on a meaning unlike any other—a lasting significance that cannot simply be taken away.

We must therefore try to understand what Iran's philosophers and spiritual teachers committed themselves to. What was the spiritual cause they had already embraced before Islam's prophetic message reached them, and how did that earlier commitment shape their reception and understanding of Islam? Shiism directs philosophical reflection above all towards the reality of the prophetic message. This “prophetic philosophy” includes an understanding of the human being that takes the Prophet and the Twelve Imams as its principal examples. Ishraq, the philosophy of illumination, is a new emergence of ancient Persia's philosophy of Light.

As the book unfolds, we shall see that the spiritual character of Islamic Iran is shaped especially by Shiism and Ishraq. Because so little of this world has been properly understood until now, it also shows us how much we still have to learn from Iranian philosophers and spiritual teachers—and what work we may need to undertake today and tomorrow, with them and for them.

I have just spoken of “prophetic philosophy.” It is striking that Persian has words of Iranian origin for both a prophet and the prophetic mission: vakhshvar, vakhshur, and payghambor, alongside the Arabic nabi and rasul. Such words already have counterparts in the Avesta, the sacred book of Zoroastrian Persia. Through Suhrawardi's Ishraq, the prophetic message of ancient Iran becomes part of the same line as the great Semitic prophets. Earlier still, Ismaili spiritual interpretation had placed Zarathustra, or Zoroaster, among the spiritual dignitaries of the age of Moses.

One could argue that this way of linking traditions does not belong to critical history. Yet it is itself a spiritual fact—one that helps explain a great deal. Above all, it illuminates what matters to us here: the Iranian search for the True Prophet and the continuing pursuit of a prophetic philosophy, a recurring form taken by Iranian spiritual consciousness.

When an Iranian teenager studies the country's pre-Islamic past at school, they are not introduced to an age of ignorance, darkness, and “idolatry”—the period known in Arabic as jahiliya. They learn instead about the legendary heroes and their deeds in Ferdowsi's Shahnameh, the Book of Kings. We shall meet some of those figures later in this book, especially in Book Two. The student also learns the name of a prophet: Zarathustra, whom we in the West call Zoroaster, following the Greeks. His name entered Western philosophical writing through figures such as Kleuker, Nietzsche, and G. T. Fechner.

Zarathustra is the earliest name that appears on the horizon of Iran's religious past, whether we place him in the tenth or the seventh century before our era. A prophet is someone who brings a divine revelation to humanity. That is how his own community traditionally understood him. It is also how he was understood within Islam by the school of Illuminationists that followed Suhrawardi. This traditional understanding has a claim to be heard in its own right; newer interpretations based on ethnology do not automatically cancel it.

Yet this book will not be about that remarkable ancient past. In an earlier work, I tried to identify certain enduring features of the Iranian vision of the world, a vision that transforms the very meaning of the earth and its landscapes. From the beginning, Iranian religious thought was guided by its clear vision of the final events that would bring the cosmic struggle to an end—a struggle set in motion by the invasion of the forces of Ahriman, the power of evil. It was the first to formulate, and continued to develop, what we may call a “philosophy of Resurrection.” I shall not return here to those enduring themes that lead “from Zoroastrian Iran to Shiite Iran.”

What we must do instead is choose a few passages from the enormous body of hadith: traditions preserving what the Shiite Imams taught their closest disciples. These teachings are deeply religious and spiritual, far removed from political claims to power. For reasons that remain mysterious, the Abbasid caliph Ma'mun (died 218 AH / 833 CE), son of Harun al-Rashid, decided to name the Eighth Imam, Ali Reza (died 203 AH / 818 CE), as his successor. This provoked furious protests from hostile members of the Hashimite family, and the Imam himself had to struggle inwardly to accept an appointment he had no power to refuse.
But the Imam died unexpectedly a year later, in circumstances that Corbin does not regard as accidental, and the extraordinary plan came to an end.

As we shall see, even well-intentioned talk of the Imams' political “legitimacy,” as descendants of Ali, turns a spiritual question into a worldly one and misses the point entirely. The closed line of Twelve Imams, whose last member remains invisibly present in this world until the end of our age, is not competing with any political dynasty. They do not even occupy the same field. We might compare them to the secret line of guardians of the Grail in Western traditions. Those guardians do not compete with any earthly royal house or even with the Church's official hierarchy and apostolic succession. They stand beyond them. The Imams, like the guardians of the Grail, belong to another world, one that cannot be reduced to social institutions or events in political history.

A teaching repeated by one Imam after another declares: “Our cause is difficult and demanding. None can bear it except an angel of the highest rank, a prophet sent by God, or a faithful believer whose heart God has tested for faith.”

We shall return to that saying, as we shall to these words of the Sixth Imam, Ja'far al-Sadiq (died 148 AH / 765 CE): “Islam began as a stranger, and it will become a stranger again, just as it was in the beginning. Blessed are the strangers among the community of Muhammad!” These “strangers” are those who leave the crowd behind to follow the Imam in spiritual worship.

Some people hear this challenge and answer yes. Their answer cannot be explained by anything other than who they are. It reflects a choice made at a level deeper than their life in this world, whose ultimate reasons escape our deductions. That assent is the living reality of Shiism. It is also the hidden message of Islam as generations of Iranian spiritual seekers have understood it, and to which they have devoted themselves with passionate faith.

Why is it, then, that when we draw attention to Shiism and its place in Islamic philosophy and spiritual life, some people whose work and calling are devoted to religion—and especially to Islam—seem surprised, even alarmed, before quickly rejecting the subject? Their first response may be that Shiism is, after all, only a “marginal Islam.” Because they prefer what seems practically effective, they announce their preference for the majority view and those who represent it.

We could answer that anyone who has lived with Shiism in Iran for several years will never have felt they were on the margins of Islam. Quite the opposite: they will have felt themselves at the heart of an intensely living spiritual reality.

But what troubles me most about this rejection is its preference for numerical majorities. It reduces spiritual reality—already so delicate and fragile among people today—to a matter of power and numbers, as though everything had to be justified by statistics. I am inclined to see this as a grave offence against the spirit itself. Sometimes it even leads to systematically negative decisions that, I can say from experience, leave our Iranian Shiite friends deeply hurt and bewildered.

It is as though outsiders had arbitrarily decided to reduce Islam to a religion of law alone: the sharia, the religious law and its outward obligations. If you point out that Islam in its fullness depends on two inseparable sides—sharia, the law, and haqiqa, the inner spiritual truth and reality—you are told that this is no longer Islam.

Yet if there is a division within Islam between the fuqaha, the scholars of religious law, and the urafa or hukama, the spiritual sages and thinkers devoted to divine wisdom, someone standing outside Islam has no right to declare that the latter do not belong to it.

Still, the answer comes back, ready-made. If you explain that the walayat of the Imams is the inner dimension of prophecy, and that Shiite irfan—Shiite spiritual knowledge—is, in a special sense, the inner knowledge of Islam itself, these same critics take fright at the very word gnosis, or direct spiritual knowledge. Their idea of what that word means is far removed from the thing itself. They then think they are entitled to push Shiism to the margins.

But in making that sweeping judgment, they would be placing the Twelve Imams, along with the countless witnesses to spiritual truth, outside Islam. We should say plainly what is at stake: spiritual Islam itself would be denied the right to be Islam.
Is that, ultimately, what these critics want? To confine Islam within the boundaries of religious law so tightly that anyone drawn to its spiritual depths has no choice but to leave it?

That would ignore the fact that the urafa and hukama found the spiritual path they sought precisely within Islam, in its inner dimension. This is what Shiism represents for those who follow the teachings of the holy Imams. Inevitably, we must now consider the relationship between Shiism and Sufism. The question will return throughout this book, including in the terms used by thinkers who were both Shiites and Sufis—above all Haydar Amoli, who lived in the eighth Islamic century, the fourteenth century of the common era.

Unfortunately, although Western scholars have studied Sufism quite extensively, and many Westerners know something about it—and people who feel spiritually lost may be drawn to it, sometimes in genuine forms and sometimes in less genuine ones—the same cannot be said of Shiism. Our understanding of Sufism is therefore incomplete and sometimes distorted. This makes it harder to grasp what the relationship between Shiism and Sufism actually involves, or why many Shiites who are themselves deeply mystical have serious reservations about Sufism.

Western readers generally know Sufism through its Sunni setting. As a result, they often see it as the only alternative to a religion built on law. Shiism, meanwhile, is explained as an attachment to the political rights of a particular family, with little thought given to what “political” might mean in different contexts. Even less effort is made to distinguish the spiritual circles around the Imams, in which the specifically religious idea of Shiism took shape—the only aspect that concerns us here—from political activists or agitators who may have used it for their own purposes, as happens with other religious ideas.

Shiism is consequently reduced, almost, to a fifth school of religious law alongside the four recognised in Sunni Islam: the Hanbali, Hanafi, Maliki, and Shafi'i schools. A similar tendency has appeared in attempts at unity within some Sunni circles. The result is a mistaken conclusion: if Shiites object to Sufism, their reasons must be the same as those of Sunni religious authorities. That is how the question gets distorted before the discussion has even begun.

The picture becomes harder still when we find Shiite spiritual thinkers such as Haydar Amoli and Mulla Sadra Shirazi having to defend themselves on two fronts. On one side stands a certain kind of Sufism; on the other, a certain kind of Shiism that is so afraid of Sufism that it retreats into a narrow legalism, forgetting what makes Shiism itself. This has been especially true since the Safavid period, when Twelver Shiism became Iran's state religion.

What both sides often forget, and what the familiar Western picture overlooks, is that most Sufi orders, or tariqas—the word means “paths”—trace their spiritual line back to a Shiite Imam, especially the First Imam, Ali ibn Abi Talib, or the Eighth Imam, Ali Reza. Even if we question the historical accuracy of particular links, the meaning of these claimed lines of descent becomes all the more revealing. Haydar Amoli will remind us, in a major work, of what Shiism and Sufism share: the relationship between prophecy and walayat, between religious law (sharia) and its spiritual meaning, and between the outward (zahir) and the inward (batin). We shall return to this in Book Four, Chapter One.

Yet it is precisely here that their differences also appear. Twelver Shiism, and Shiite spiritual knowledge in particular, has sought to maintain the balance and simultaneous presence of outward and inward meaning, of symbol and what it symbolises. Certain forms of Sufism, by contrast, have often disturbed that balance.

One sign of this imbalance lies in the importance Sufi orders give to their shaykh, or spiritual teacher. The shaykh may be treated as the qutb, the spiritual “pole,” and effectively recognised as the Imam's visible embodiment and successor. A Shiite Sufi teacher such as Sa'd al-Din Hamuyi (died 650 AH / 1252 CE) could have a particularly deep devotion to the Twelfth, Hidden Imam. But in other circumstances, devotion to the shaykh may diminish the significance of the Hidden Imam himself.

For a Shiite whose spirituality centres on the Imam, that is intolerable. It amounts to a kind of usurpation, often accompanied by excessive devotion to the shaykh. More importantly, it violates the spiritual situation created by the Imam's occultation (ghayba)—his withdrawal from ordinary human sight—which is to continue until the end of our present age. Paradoxically, Sufism can then appear to turn the deepest spiritual truths of Shiism into something dependent on a visible human figure.
In this way Sufism would tend to remove the teaching about the Imams altogether. In Sunni Sufism, that is ultimately what happens.

But the balance between outer and inner meaning can be preserved only through the corresponding balance between prophecy and walayat: between the understanding of prophets and the understanding of Imams. The balance is destroyed when the particular spiritual gifts of the Imam are simply transferred to the Prophet. Without a place for the Imam, an authentic understanding of God's oneness—tawhid, the recognition of the One beyond all others—also becomes impossible. Such understanding must avoid two opposing dangers: ta'til, which empties the idea of God into a distant, unknowable abstraction, and tashbih, which makes God too much like a human being. We shall return to both in Chapters Six and Seven.

Now we can see why a Shiite spiritual seeker may regard a Sunni Sufi as someone who has forgotten their own origins. We can also see why that same Shiite might worry that even Shiite Sufism threatens something deeply precious. The Shiite seeker does not necessarily need Sufism, its organised orders, or its shaykhs. Through a personal inward bond with the holy Imams, that person is already travelling a spiritual path, without needing the path to take the visible form of a Sufi order. Their words may sound exactly like those of a Sufi, yet they may belong to no Sufi order at all. Mulla Sadra Shirazi could even write a fairly severe treatise against the Sufis of his own day.

Once we understand this, we may stop misreading major Sufis such as Hallaj, or the relationship between Hallaj and Muhyiddin Ibn Arabi. We misunderstand both the meaning and the place of spiritual knowledge in Islam when we insist that Hallaj was simply a faithful Sunni with no connection to it. This is a Western way of seeing things, barely concealing a wish to defend a particular theological position. It decides in advance that the texts must show Hallaj and Ibn Arabi to be opposites—as though Ibn Arabi were a “monist,” believing that reality is ultimately one, while Hallaj were not.

In truth, either both were monists or neither was. If we use the Western philosophical term monism in its precise sense, neither was. Ruzbihan of Shiraz remains our best guide to understanding Hallaj; Ibn Arabi, in turn, was in a better position than we are to understand what was at stake. Neither Hallaj nor Ibn Arabi sought to “go beyond” Islam or leave it behind, any more than Ghazali did when he worked to bring the mystical life into Sunni Islam. They lived through Islam and brought its hidden spiritual power into actual life. What they did go beyond was a purely legal, social, and political understanding of Islam—an understanding that would, in fact, be the death of its spiritual life.

A Shiite spiritual thinker is particularly well placed to understand Hallaj's tragedy, his preoccupation with the figure of Iblis, and the complexity of Ibn Arabi's life and work. Haydar Amoli will remind us of this again. If Christian teachings about Christ become relevant to our discussion, it is not because Hallaj secretly converted to some Christian “religion of the Cross.” It is because the Shiite teaching about the Imams plays a role in Shiite theology comparable to the role played by teachings about Christ in Christian theology.

Shiite thinkers have often drawn parallels between the Imam and Jesus. For example, Jesus is described as the Seal of the walayat that begins with Adam; the First Imam as the Seal of universal walayat; and the Twelfth Imam as the Seal of the walayat associated with Muhammad. This helps explain those extraordinary sermons in which the Imam calls himself “the second Christ.” We shall also encounter the dreams of the Twelfth Imam's mother in Book Seven.

Whenever Shiite thought about the Imams has faced questions like those faced by Christian thought about Christ, it has tended to adopt answers resembling positions rejected by the Christian councils. But the comparison also shows how flimsy a common theological classification really is: the attempt to divide all religious experience into “natural” and “supernatural” theology or mysticism.

It is far too convenient to lump together under “natural mysticism,” or “Yoga-type mysticism,” spiritual teachings that have little in common. In this scheme, “natural” mysticism means a person trying to unite with an impersonal Absolute, or impersonal Self, through their own powers. “Supernatural” theology, concerned with divine grace, supposedly offers another kind of relationship. However worthy the religious aims behind this division may be, Islamic divine wisdom—irfan and hikmat—has a range of thought and practice broad enough to reject so simple a split.

The Islamic idea of prophecy and the prophetic mission, which does not mean “predicting the future,” certainly cannot be reduced to the model of Yoga. It embraces the whole line of prophets found in the Bible and sees that line continued in Muhammad, who was so deeply attentive to the earlier scriptural revelations. If “natural” religion means a human effort to achieve salvation by one's own strength, neither the prophetic gift nor the spiritual gift of the Imams depends on such effort.

That is precisely why Shiite theology insists that, although people can choose a head of state or establish a religious office, they cannot elect a prophet or an Imam. The very idea is absurd. Nor does a meeting with the Hidden Imam—a form that an unexpected encounter with divine help or grace can take in Shiism—come about simply through human effort. It is no more a union with an impersonal Self than prophecy is. The very meanings of “natural” and “temporal” are transformed.

Through meditation on the Qur'an, Shiite spiritual thinkers are able to embrace the whole cycle of prophecy and religion. Even the Greek sages, for example, are said to have received their wisdom from the “niche of lights” of prophecy. These traditions form the “six days” in which the religious cosmos is created, and these thinkers know that a seventh day will come.

By contrast, is it unfair to speak of the difficulties that official Christian thought has faced in creating a theology of religions broad enough to recognise the sacred book in its full reality, even when that revelation takes the form of the Qur'an? Why raise questions like this? Because in our time we can no longer honestly avoid them. They arise inevitably as soon as we ask, as we are doing here, what we have to learn from Iranian philosophers and spiritual teachers, and what we might do with them and for them. How could we discuss the “spirituality of Iranian Islam” while remaining silent about all this?

At the centre of Islam in its fullest spiritual sense lies the tension between sharia—religious law and the outward duties of faith—and haqiqa, the inward spiritual truth: the deeper understanding of scripture and the discovery of hidden meanings belonging to higher levels of existence and awareness. Both sides are essential. I believe this is entirely true to the outlook of the spiritual sages of Twelver Shiism. Remove either side, and the fullness of Islamic religious life disappears.

Haqiqa is the inner truth of the outward religion, which it therefore presupposes. It is not a licence to do whatever one likes in the name of spiritual freedom. If something is forbidden, discovering its deeper meaning does not make it permitted: the inner meaning of what is forbidden remains connected to a real prohibition. Conversely, religious law without inner spiritual truth is not thereby “saved.” It becomes an empty shell.

If the tension between the two is abolished by removing the inward dimension, we also lose the idea of the purely spiritual community held together by an invisible bond. Religious truth is then identified completely with a social system. And when the structure of traditional society begins to break apart, the very idea of religion is thrown into crisis.

To bring these introductory reflections to a close, I shall turn in the next section to a moving example of what happens when spiritual life is absorbed into society in a Sunni Muslim setting. It leads us to ask whether the situation in Shiite Islam might be different.

At first sight, one essential difference stands out. In Shiism, walayat and the Imamate are understood as inseparable from prophecy and as its necessary continuation. The prophetic mission and the Imamate of the Twelve arise together. In the Shiite understanding, the Imamate is the original and enduring support of haqiqa: the spiritual truth that gives sharia its life. It keeps interpretation of the Qur'an open to other worlds of meaning, as we shall see in Chapters Four and Five, and it keeps that interpretation open to the future.

Without the Imamate, by contrast, any search for haqiqa loses its footing. It lacks a guide and a point of reference by which to steer between the twin dangers of ta'til and tashbih: an agnostic rationalism that leaves God unknowable, and a naive tendency to imagine God in human form.

Let me make this clearer. The Imams are no longer physically present in this world. Their authority cannot even be compared with the often ambiguous authority of a visible “spiritual power” that can place demands on human souls. What matters is their spiritual presence: the Imam as an inward guide to consciousness, and, at the highest level, as the figure who shapes the horizon of our understanding of reality. That is what it means to call the Imam the Guide, the Pole, and the Witness. We shall return to this in Chapter Seven.

In the new world now taking shape, with more and more of the marks of an age of iron, the Prophet's religion risks being stifled and destroyed only if it is forcibly cut off from its spiritual truth and the interpretation that keeps that truth alive. The Imams repeatedly warned against the error of reducing scripture to the time of its revelation. If every Qur'anic verse meant only what it meant for the people and events to which it first referred, the whole Qur'an would already be dead, nothing but a record of the past.

But the Book is alive because its events continue to unfold within human souls, right up to Yawm al-Qiyama, the Day of Resurrection. Its living meaning cannot be tied to one moment of history or to the social order of any particular time and place. Only people who live by the spirit can understand, perceive, and say this. To say that sharia can survive only through haqiqa is to say that spiritual truth alone can bring about the changes needed to keep religion alive, rather than allowing politics and social pressures to distort and suffocate it.

The danger is not confined to Islam. Every religion, Christianity included, risks surrendering its spiritual life to social concerns and institutions. The danger begins within us, when people abandon their own spiritual responsibility and allow themselves to become part of that surrender. Confusing religion with society is hardly a new mistake. Those who will withstand it are not people searching for compromises with “their age,” but those strong enough to become shuhada: witnesses who speak against their age, bearing witness to another world—and to a world that is different even here. To announce that other reality is the heart of the prophetic message.

Neither people nor books can manufacture witnesses like these. But we can at least ask the questions that matter. Will there be, tomorrow, people capable of carrying the inner truth of Islam, so that the meaning of a purely spiritual Islam—one that has nothing to do with the schemes and ambitions of politicians—can become visible in our world?

That question speaks especially to Shiism. At the beginning of its religious year, the remembrance of the tragedy of Karbala is a continuing protest against the powers of this world. And Shiism's hope for the return of the Hidden Imam, which shapes its spiritual life, shows that this question has confronted it from its beginning. Will Shiism still be able to make its voice heard tomorrow, as it did when only a handful of believers stood beside the Imams? We shall return to this in Chapter Three.

I have just spoken about what happens when spiritual life is absorbed into social life, and about the effects this has on a traditional culture. These effects place a heavy responsibility on everyone who refuses to take part in what, more than a generation ago, was rightly called “the betrayal of the intellectuals.” We hear that expression less often today. Yet surely the betrayal cannot be allowed to become final.

In the West, we have come to realise that many of our social and political ideologies are really forms of theology that have lost their religious character. They grew out of earlier systems of theological thought, but removed the message of a world beyond this one. However far human hopes may reach, they no longer pass beyond death.

We can see this change particularly clearly when religious hopes for a saving figure and a final renewal of the world become hopes for nothing more than social transformation. Once our vision of the end of history has been stripped of its religious meaning, what remains is a story about the supposed “direction of history.”

This did not happen overnight. It was a long process. Turning religion into something secular does not simply mean replacing religious authorities with worldly rulers. The very idea of a “spiritual power” made into institutions and exercised as a form of power is already a step towards turning the spiritual into something worldly and social. That process begins when every form of spiritual knowledge is attacked, as happened for centuries. By cutting itself off from gnosis—knowledge of spiritual realities reached through direct understanding—the institutional Church failed to see that it was preparing the way for an age of agnosticism and a belief that only observable facts count as knowledge.

The authority of religious doctrine was simply replaced by the social authority of shared rules. The person once condemned as a “heretic” became someone accused of “deviation,” or simply someone said to be “maladjusted.” Individual religious experience and every kind of mystical life could now be explained away as a failure to fit into one's social environment. The automatic refusal to recognise what lies beyond ordinary knowledge prevents us from welcoming witnesses to “another world.”

It is painful to see how much of Christianity today is haunted by a particular fear: the fear of being seen as not belonging to “this world,” and therefore of not being taken seriously. People exhaust themselves trying to “keep up with the times,” proclaiming the “priority of social concerns,” and bringing themselves into line with supposed “scientific requirements.” In this frantic race, they lose sight of what matters most. Nikolai Berdyaev identified the tragedy: in its official historical forms, Christianity has given in to the very temptation that Christ rejected.

Yet these secular forms of theology are exactly what the West carries with it wherever it goes, along with the machinery of its material civilisation. By “the West,” I mean both what our newspapers call the West and what they call the East. Many people living in the geographical East are now “Western” in the sense I am using, sometimes more so than people in the geographical West who have not yet lost their bearings. But what happens when these imported ways of thinking reach societies that never had the earlier theological structures from which they developed?

The problem is especially serious for Islam, because Islam and Christianity share the foundations of a prophetic religion. Both honour the names and teachings of many of the same prophets. Yet, as I have noted more than once, the goal of Islamic philosophers and spiritual thinkers has been neither what we usually call theology nor exactly what we usually call philosophy. Their hikmat ilahiya is divine wisdom: a phrase whose two parts correspond directly to the Greek roots of theosophia.

In fact, we could say that separating theology from philosophy is itself the first sign that consciousness is becoming secular. In the West, that separation goes back to Latin scholastic thought, perhaps to Thomas Aquinas's Summa contra Gentiles. Theology becomes the territory reserved for an official “spiritual power,” while philosophy claims every freedom except the freedom to be theology. Here we see the first sign of a world in which even our understanding of reality loses its sacred character.

Divine wisdom, theosophia, is the opposite of that process and its antidote. It can be lived only through what these thinkers call knowledge of the heart (ma'rifat qalbiya), which is why that idea matters so much to Shiite philosophers of divine wisdom. In this way of knowing, theoretical understanding and spiritual experience cannot be separated. Only their union can turn everything a person learns and does into deeper understanding and awareness of the self. That may well be what people today need most.

We should not be surprised, then, that whenever Islamic divine wisdom has faced questions resembling those of Christian theology, it has tended towards answers close in spirit to certain forms of Christianity—particularly those forms pushed “to the margins of history,” to use a fashionable expression, by the decisions of official religious authorities. We have already seen an example of this in Shiite thought about the Imams.

We might now ask where the real dividing lines lie. Do they run between the established religions, or do people with similar spiritual outlooks find one another within those religions, sometimes without their institutions even noticing? Recognising these deeper connections would help us avoid serious misunderstandings. Well-meaning specialists working in another culture sometimes fail to see the inner collapse brought about when people are overwhelmed by ideas that did not grow out of their own experience. Nor do they understand the private ways in which others protect themselves, including their refusal to answer an investigator's intrusive questions. Recognising these connections would also help genuinely spiritual people see what unites them, understand the problems they share, and perhaps confront those problems together for the first time.

A few pages ago, we spoke of the tension between sharia and haqiqa: the outward requirements of revealed religion and its inner spiritual truth. We can shut ourselves inside the outward form and, by rejecting the inner truth, diminish even that outward form. Or we can devote ourselves to the inner truth and thereby preserve the full meaning of the outward practice. We have seen that this second approach lies at the heart of Twelver Shiism and the teaching of its Imams.

But the same tension belongs to what I have called the experience of having a sacred Book. It is familiar to all the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab). Judaism and Christianity, too, have traditions concerned with hidden spiritual meanings, and these have much in common with the seekers of inner knowledge in Islam.

It would be a fascinating undertaking—enormous in scale, with consequences we cannot foresee—to compare the place and history of these inner traditions in Islam and Christianity. We would have to go back to Gnosis, the search for saving spiritual knowledge. We would need to consider the teachings Christ gave his closest disciples, reread the recently recovered Gnostic Gospels with fresh eyes, and ask how certain Gospel passages and sayings, often quoted by Shiite and Ismaili writers, reached them through Gnostic channels or acquired a Gnostic colouring along the way. By “fresh eyes,” I mean approaching Gnosis without a prejudice against it. Ignorance cannot excuse every misunderstanding.

What we usually call “Gnosticism” would then appear as one expression of a much wider religious experience: gnosis, or knowledge that brings salvation. It is knowledge because it involves being initiated into a teaching. It brings salvation because the mystery of higher worlds, concealed beneath the words of divine revelations, cannot truly be disclosed or understood without a new birth in the person who receives it—a spiritual birth, called wiladat ruhaniya in Arabic.
We are still far from having gathered all the surviving writings and evidence of this wider Gnostic religious tradition into an accessible collection.

Yet seekers of spiritual knowledge, wherever and whenever they have lived, share another characteristic: they resist a faith based solely on historical evidence, what Latin calls fides historica. Such faith judges how real something is by whether documents can show that it existed physically in the past—or insists on reading documents as proof of that kind. It demands a securely established place in ordinary chronology, just as it would for any event or person in secular history.
